content:
Out of the workshop # Molecule is where I bring my interests in software, light, and physical interaction together. The pop-up at Moongoat Coffee was a chance to take that work into a shared space.
The setup brought together illuminated sword props, a camera and vertical display, and a small LED face display. The invitation was simple: come play with swords and motion capture.
A connection you can see # I’m interested in experiences where the relationship between a person’s movement and what they see feels immediate. Light and a physical object offer a different starting point from a conventional screen interface. The object, the visual response, and the space around the participant all become part of the work.
Building the tools to make it # My independent embedded work includes ESP32 firmware, motion sensor data, networking, and LED experiments. Alongside the physical work, I build the software and tools needed to explore those connections.
This exploration continues through Molecule’s light and sensor projects, with the pop-up forming one chapter in that practice.
Related experience # At Enflux, I developed motion capture applications and tools that connected people to real-time software and animation workflows. My film-set work brought software and visuals into physical production environments. Those experiences inform the independent work I make as Molecule.
summary: Out of the workshop # Molecule is where I bring my interests in software, light, and physical interaction together. The pop-up at Moongoat Coffee was a chance to take that work into a shared space.
title: Light you can move

content:
Software in a physical scene # At Paper Ghost, I developed interactive media for film and television: software, screen visuals, and animation that had to work within a real production. The work involved collaborating with directors, producers, VFX supervisors, and set crews under tight deadlines.
The challenge was both visual and practical. An interface had to support the scene, read well on camera, and provide the behavior needed by a performer or operator.
X-Men: Apocalypse # I created software and digital visuals for the Pentagon video wall and retro computer screens. The work included maps, timers, clocks, and control displays that helped build the environment seen on camera.
The production was a collaboration. My responsibilities covered software and visual content, while Zed Axiz supplied hardware and set operators.
The Glass Castle # I programmed playback software for a rear projection installation used to shoot driving scenes in a studio. The tools supported 4K/360° video, color calibration, video warping, and wireless playback control from an Android tablet.
This was software designed around the relationship between projected imagery, a physical set, a camera, and the person operating it.
The Glass Castle: rear projection playback in a physical studio setup. My contribution was the video software and its controls. Interactive props and virtual cameras # For Quantico, I developed actor-operated phone and screen applications, including scripted calls, messages, surveillance displays, and timers. For Arrival, I programmed tools to customize military maps and surveillance screen content.
For mother!, I programmed a set previsualization application for framing shots and blocking performers. It included a virtual camera tool using real-world measurements and physically based lens settings, with desktop and Gear VR versions.
What carries into my practice # These projects taught me to work closely with creative collaborators and to think beyond the application window. The software needed to fit the space, the equipment, and the story being told.
More production imagery and earlier work →
summary: Software in a physical scene # At Paper Ghost, I developed interactive media for film and television: software, screen visuals, and animation that had to work within a real production.
title: Part of the scene

content:
A moving person as the input # At Enflux, I built software that connected motion capture clothing to interactive applications and creative workflows. The work ranged from a Unity SDK for developers to first-party applications and live demonstrations.
The interesting part was the connection: turning the movement of a person into something that an application, artist, or participant could use.
Enflux motion capture clothing. I developed the SDK, applications, and creative tools that used its motion data. Tools for developers and artists # I shipped the Unity SDK used by business partners and consumer developers to work with the motion capture clothing. I also developed a Blender plugin to record motion captured animation and export FBX files.
A companion Unity-based Windows application sent smooth motion data over Wi-Fi to Blender on other computers. This connected the real-time capture experience with an animation workflow beyond the demo itself.
Bringing it in front of people # My work included first-party applications, investor demonstrations, workshops, tech talks, and hackathons. I also managed trade show booths for CES, SVVR, and SIGGRAPH.
Demonstrating an interactive application in person makes the relationship between input and response especially important. The software has to communicate what it does through the experience itself.
My contribution # My responsibilities covered software, SDKs, applications, and creative tooling, working alongside the team developing the motion capture clothing.
That experience informs my ongoing light and motion work as Molecule.
summary: A moving person as the input # At Enflux, I built software that connected motion capture clothing to interactive applications and creative workflows. The work ranged from a Unity SDK for developers to first-party applications and live demonstrations.
title: Movement as an interface

content:
Engineering that supports creative work # My work on Hearthstone at Blizzard covered the core technology that helps a creative game run, grow, and reach players across platforms. It brought together engine behavior, content delivery, performance constraints, and the tools used by other disciplines.
Content and artist tools # I maintained and improved the asset pipeline used to pack and ship the game’s content worldwide. My responsibilities also included client build tooling and tools for FX artists.
I care about the connection between making creative content and getting that content into a working experience. The tools and pipeline affect what artists can make and how easily a team can iterate.
Core engine and platform work # My responsibilities included memory and download performance, native mobile development, SDK integrations, and low-level engine issues. I also supported engineers on other teams with guidance and solutions to blocking problems.
Multi-platform development makes the constraints concrete: the same creative work needs to reach people using different devices and operating environments.
How it connects # My current engineering focus includes 3D graphics techniques, rendering, and content pipeline tools for art and audio.
This experience supports the engineering side of my creative practice: understanding rendering and runtime constraints, building tools for other people, and carrying work through to delivery. Together with film-set experience and motion capture tools, it informs the way I approach interactive work as Molecule.
summary: Engineering that supports creative work # My work on Hearthstone at Blizzard covered the core technology that helps a creative game run, grow, and reach players across platforms. It brought together engine behavior, content delivery, performance constraints, and the tools used by other disciplines.
title: Behind the creative world

I did a graphics pass to come up with a stylistic direction I’m much happier with.I’m working through the process to correctly convert the motion capture data to look good on the robot, which will likely take months to get “good enough” looking.
I also recorded reference poses to start iterating on the math quickly. This is faster than having to mocap myself everytime I test a code change.
Instead of hacking something together, I stepped back and started planning “what I’d really like” in Miro for a more polished process.

content:
Testing procedural animation based on sacred geometry rules.CREATION # Designed and programmed in Unity Engine 2019.4.2 using C# and Shader Graph. The animation is created by making a graph data structure. The root node branches into 6 equidistant subtrees, forming a starfish.
Each child node is the inverse golden ratio of the parent’s scale.
Golden Ratio (φ) # \(\varphi = \dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}= 1.6180339887…\)
Inverse Golden Ratio (1/φ) # \(\dfrac{1}{\varphi} = 0.61803398875…\)
Constant rotation is applied to spin the shape. Rotation speed is a multiple of the golden ratio.
SHADING # A fresnel effect is used to create a rim glow effect.
See Godot Engine example:
Transparency is oscillated by using a sine function.
Constant rotation is applied to an angled directional light, creating the eclipse effect. Rotation speed is a multiple of the golden ratio.
Video is captured on a phone to create a retro light-bleeding effect.
MUSIC # Song is a lo-fi remix of “In Search of the Man in Black” from Final Fantasy VII:
Ｃｈａｓｉｎｇ ｔｈｅ Ｃａｐｅｄ Ｍａｎ(Kannibal)
summary: Testing procedural animation based on sacred geometry rules.CREATION # Designed and programmed in Unity Engine 2019.4.2 using C# and Shader Graph. The animation is created by making a graph data structure.
